text: Now that I have finished the game, for me it has an overall fun gameplay and poor character/story development. So: I didn't expect a very thoughful story from a shooter like this, but I did expect at least the couple of interesting ideas presented in the trailer being developed a bit. Instead, they went rather deep in the plot while combining it with a huge amount of clichés: character stereotypes, sexism, character realationships, race clichés... so the whole thing didn't work for me. You can't take a serious plot and drive it with this kind of script. The dialogues and reactions are unnatural and the relationships progress (good or bad) escalate too quickly. The trust meter mechanic is useless for me and the options to choose too vague so I ended up choosing always the one on the bottom of the list. text: Binary Domain doesn't really add anything new to the shooter genre, but it executes on established mechanics extremely well. The shooting is extremely satisfying with chunks of metal flying off your robotic foes with each bullet. Enemy behavior changes depending on where you shoot them. Shooting off a leg causes a robot to crawl at you for a close attack while shooting off a robot's head causes it to shoot at friend and foe alike. Other features such as purchaseable upgrades for your guns, your character, and your allies help enhance the sense of progress through the game. There is trust system in the game that aims to add a sense of depth and connection to your NPC allies. Trust isn't very important to the core gameplay, but having a certain trust level with certain allies does affect your game ending, which adds some replayability. Binary Domain is a strong 3rd person shooter with a great story, corny writing, and fun characters.

text: It's Meh I've heard lots of good things about this game, so I bought it during the Steam Winter Sale. I did not enjoy this game. At first, the game was pretty fun, and I liked it, though I noticed a delay from when I hit a key to when the game responded (I had no lag/framedrop during the time of play) so it made the game difficult to stay on beat, so I found myself starting over quite a bit. This could just be my keyboard, so I don't know. Also, there are no checkpoints. At all. So one little mistake, one little off-beat press of a button, and you are sent all the way back through that 5 minute level you just drudged through. The game itself is a music/rythm platforming game, however I wouldn't call it a rythm game. It feels more like a memory game. Throughout the game, you must jump, kick, slide, bounce, and reflect to reach the end of the stage. The graphics made me felt like I was going crosseyed while I played, they look good, but they don't mix well with a moving foreground. It made it unenjoyable, and I got headaches from it. This, mixed with the whole jumping and kicking, made it nearly impossible for me to even see what was going on. The rounds would drag on, and on. So, I had to memorize the course, while the backround remains stationary with a moving foreground, with a delay on me hitting buttons. Here is the most enjoying part. The music. I loved it, except, every time you die, you get sent back to the beginning. Meaning that the music starts over with it. So you will be hearing the same du-du-dun-dun-dun-du-dun ... du-du-dun-dun-dun-du-dun ... du-du-dun-dun-dun-du-dun over and over again. I know I said I loved the music, but I couldn't love it enough from the constant restarting. Also, a lot of the songs sound the same, the music is put together from you "staying on beat" with the music. Staying on beat is used loosely (see above paragraph). I liked this aspect, you were making the music as you played along. The music progressively got better and better as you played, unless you miss one of those power-ups that up you, and the music. That part bugged me, but it is my fault for not being good enough, it made me want to replay the level and try to hear the music to it's full potential. The graphics, they are really good. It's a mix of a stationary backround and a moving foreground, which I hated, but even though I hated how they pulled it off, they looked very good. So credit where it's due. So, to close this review, here are the pros and cons of this game. Good music, good graphics, fun to play, bonus levels are repetetive, but fun, a bit of replay value in there. Repetetive music, headache inducing graphics, late controls, lack of checkpoints makes the game very unforgiving, not a rythym but instead a memory game.  I did not enjoy BIT.TRIP RUNNER and I do not believe it is worth the $10 it is being sold for currently. I'm glad I paid for it during the sale for much, much, cheaper. I have no words for the sequel, as I have not played it. Some may find it okay, if they don't have the late controls or headaches, but I did not like BIT.TRIP RUNNER.

title: blackguards
text: It should be noted that I picked up this game in a sale at a discounted price, my opinion is based on me paying about £18 for it rather than the full price. I think it is likely that my opinion on this game would change if I had forked out £30 for it. I knew about Daedlic's point and click games like Deponia so I was interested to see what their take on a RPG would be like. As it is something that I almost expect in a RPG nowdays it is important to state that this game is very linear. If you are expecting something like Dragon Age you are going to be very disapointed (to be fair expecting all RPGs to be like Dragon Age will invaribly lead to disappointment). Also I think the game description is a bit misleading, you and your companions do have a slight criminal air about yourselves but at the end of the day it is standard save the world type stuff, nothing too ground breaking. The game has three main views, the first is the world overview you use for travelling around. This is basically a map type view with marker locations for villages, towns, places of interest etc... To move around you click on where you want to go and jump to that location - so no player controlled wilderness exploration or anything like that. The next view is the "town view". This is pretty much a static view where you can click on characters to buy goods or obtain/advance quests. The final view is the battle view, this is a map split up into small hexagons where the player controlled combat takes place. These battle maps range in size, though none are particularly huge. They consist of different environments and obstacles that sometimes require a change in tactics for some scenarios. Combat is turn based attack and move type stuff with close combat with swords, axes, maces etc..., ranged with bows and crossbows and ranged with magic. The combat can get a bit repetitious but there is enough in there that it does not feel too much a grind. You get to pick one of three classes for your main character, a mage, a rogue/archer type or a fighter. On levelling up you pick attributes and combat skills and there is the freedom to create hybrid classes by giving your archer some mage abilities for example. I did find though that each class tends to have one particularly powerful skill or skill combo that you will just tend to repeat in combat. The game itself has a lot of good and bad points, it is quite a mixed bag but there is probably going to be something in there that does end up annoying you, it certainly is not perfect. How much that thing annoys you is probably the defining factor in whether you will ultimately enjoy the game or not. For me it was with the combat, there are some monsters which are only vunerable to one type of damage. However, ahead of the battle you do not necessarily know what type of monster you will be fighting so in my case I frequently had everyone inflicting either piercing or magic damage. That was my best set up given my characters, weapons and prefered skills. However, in some fights monsters will be invulnerable to piercing so you have to quit the game reload and re-equip characters with maces so you can inflict bashing damage. Nothing game breaking but it did really get annoying, you learn pretty early on to have back up weapons handy and make sure your party is at least a bit flexible. You can look on that as somewhat of a positive as my party was really not set up for those particular battles so it did add an extra challenge, making what should have been an easy fight a bit more difficult. I think one other problem that needs highlighting is the party make up. You have a limited number of companions that you can recruit, essentially there is one party for the game. You do not get to deicde if you would rather have a mage or a fighter in your party you get what your are given. I do not want to spoil anything but at some point in the game something happens that means that really to fill a specific gap in your party your main character needs to be a specific class. Luckily I chose this class anyway so it was not a problem in my play through. If I had selected a different class it may have negatively effected my opinion of the game. On the positive side I liked the story (the ending is a bit meh but nothing too objectionable) and found the characters interesting with some nice back story and different personalities. By the end I found myself invested in the story and felt fairly satisfied with the experience on completion. You do get some "choices with consequences moments" that give you a sense of control over how the story plays out. My play through took me 26 hours and I pretty much did everything quest wise in the game. I would recommend this game but I did pay about £18 for it. if I had paid the full retail price I would probably not recommend it as I think at that price some of the problems I have glossed over would have seemed a lot more annoying. My advice is to pick this up if you see it discounted as on the whole it is a relatively enjoyable experience. However, at full price there a lot better RPGs out there and I would be a lot less forgiving of the game's flaws.

text: This is a turn based tactics game where you control (after about 30 hours gameplay) up to 5 heroes who walk between nodes on a world map in a very linear way and follow a more or less entertaining story (At least I found some of the dialogue mildly enjoyable). Some nodes are cities where you may learn skills, buy equipment, and get/perform quests, other nodes are quest nodes that may sometimes be skipped. Most of the time is however spent in  hexagon based maps fighting various bad guys. The game has a lot of skills and stats that you may experiment with, but mostly it makes little difference what you chose to skill up (For spells any nuke will do, some early bosses are weak to fire, but it makes little difference for most enemies, a healing spell is pretty much required, you will alternate between those two and auto attacks for the whole game), and as most stats and skills are needed in the end anyway the customization adds little depth to a shallow game. The major problem with Blackguards is that fights are mostly based on luck. Want to attack someone? Well, usually you have a 90% chance to hit (not bad, but that's as good as it gets unless someone is knocked down), but if you use a more powerful attack it might drop down to 85%, 70%, or 60% (based on dodge stat vs dexterity I think), further reduced with wounds that are randomly obtained when taking damage (I think your to hit chance can potentially go all the way down to 30%). If you manage to hit at all the damage dealt is then further randomed in a fairly large spread, and rarely it will crit for double damage. The damage is fairly high, so 3-4 good attacks is enough to drop most enemies and heroes. This means that missing more than a few attacks will result in one of your heroes getting knocked unconscious, and the enemies snowball from there. It's typically the enemies who get the good dodge stats, so while your heroes will mostly take full damage from anything that attacks them late game, your heroes will miss, miss, miss,miss, and miss some more as you watch them slowly die in frustration. The game's "difficulty" slowly ramps up as you play. Every encounter is level (in)appropriate, so every fight is a challenge. Since spell damage is fixed your magic users slowly get weaker after their 2 main spells hit level 3. While this makes sense in a way you will never get to be satisfied with how much stronger your heroes have gotten. Enemies have about the same stats and skills and do about as much damage as the heroes do, so fights vary little in practise between various encounters. The game could still be a mildly enjoyable grind with the above mentioned issues, but clearly the devs were obsessed with making the game into a never ending series of encounters by a power tripping DM trying to make your party lose. I got through several unfair fights like Running past all the enemies who get to hit you for free for 6 turns to get to the girl before she's killed, shoot a giant tree with 150 hp to death with arrows that each do 1 dmg because it 2 shots everything in melee range, run through a basement filled with traps to get to the guy you need to kill before he gets away, kill the necromancer who's surrounded by unkillalbe skeletons that block your spells and arrows, and many many more. The straw that broke the camel's back for me was the fight against the tiger lilly where one of your heroes is turned against you, you have to run up to a plant that always has a 60% hit chance, is immune to magic damage, every turn one of your heroes is knocked down, and 5-6 tentacles you're not supposed to kill get to attack your heroes freely while blocking off healing spells you might want to cast on the hero being bullied. I understand that something like this was necessary to make the game interesting, as the fights by themselves clearly aren't. With a different combat system these fights might have been fun, but in Blackguards you will just keep doing the right thing again and again untill it finally works and you get to go on. So, TL;DR: Turn based fights heavily based on luck, little customization in practise despite the wealth of options available, you get weaker as you keep on playing, and gimmicky fights where the devs metaphorically throw your miss chance and weakness in your face again and again by setting up scenarios that force you into doing stupid things over and over untill the RNG gods decide that you may finally pass. If it sounds like your cup of tea then you will probably enjoy Blackguards, but I did not.

text: I really wanted to like this game.  I am a big fan of D&D and have played more RPGs than I can count.  I am also a huge fan on XCOM and that style of strategy so this looked like a match made in game heaven. Alas it was not to be though.  Here is the good the bad and the ugly. Good: - Graphics are wonderful. - Voice acting is top-notch. - There "appears" to be a lot of character customizations. Bad: - Storyline beats you up in the second chapter and you lose your "investment" arbitrarily.  Sad really. - There really is a lack of "strategy" as you are at the whim of roll of the dice.  Not XCOM calibre, not even close. - $39.99?  I got is pre-release cheap.  Save your money it isn't worth that much. Ugly: - XCOM style strategy doesn't play as such.  Random roll really makes this a flawed game.  You can employ the exact same strategy move for move and breeze through a level, and other times get decimated. - There is no place to "grind" it out to build up your characters if you are so willing to do so.  Early in the game you will find yourself redoing levels because you got a bad roll and you haven't enough Ducats (money) to do what you need. - Some levels (first one) become closed the moment you go to another map.  There is no turning back until later.  A big map, but very linear and very unforgiving. You have to REALLY love D&D style play to get into this game.  It will take a while to get used to, and even longer to become skilled at this game.  It feels more like work and less like fun. I would not buy this game again.

text: I would first like to pre-face this review by saying that I bought this Deluxe version and Blackguards 2 as part of the Daedalic bundle for £9.99, making each game in effect worth £4.99 to me. Based on this price I think Blackguards is definitely worth it. The full price of £29.99 is however WAY off the mark for the amount of game you get (hint: not much) Despite me finishing the game in 40 hours, it is a very combat focused where pretty much every event you’ll encounter will be a fight. Whilst this is fun to begin with, as a lot of battle maps are quite interesting, after 20 odd hours it just got tiresome. After every cut scene, conversation, exploration, etc I knew I would be fighting something. So you can imagine my utter delight when after defeating the final boss, the final cut-scene was just that a cut-scene! Outside of combat there is unfortunately very little to the game, hence I only recommend it at a steep discount. There is no exploration to speak off, the town screens are static and the story kind of gets lots amongst 180 fight scenes you’ll have to slog through. I also have a few gripes about the story, but these could just be personal preferences. For example, I don’t see how this is a “dark” story as it seems very much like any other RPG where you-are-our-only-hope-to-save-the-world story (spoiler: you save it). Also this games is called Blackguards and makes the point of your character being an outlaw. I was picturing more of a vagabond, a mercenary on the run, or some petty thief down and on his luck. What I wasn’t expecting however was for my character to be buddies with a PRINCES whilst chilling at a home of a COUNT in the first “memory” cutscene. Less of a BlackGuard, more of a Brodude! Also in this game you have no meaningful choice – it really just railroads you along the main story-line with some side-quests where you have a choice between killing guy A or guy B... with no impact on main story-line. A lot of negative reviews about this game are regarding the dodgy RNG, and whilst I have encountered some odd miss on a 95% chance, I have never experienced a 3 in a row miss. If you read the manual and understand how the rules work. The % you see isn’t the % to inflict damage, but rather to do an action, then the enemy gets a couple of saving rolls – parry / dodge. So you might have successfully rolled an action, but then the enemy might have rolled a saving throw and so all you see is your guy missing or spell fizzing out.

text: The first time I came to write a review for this game it was going to be a vitriolic missive of woe and anger. In true fashion, and not for the first time, the game had put me on my♥♥♥♥♥ It was during the games infamous second chapter, where fights come thick and fast, and leave you feeling brutalised and frustrated. I perservered however and came out of the other side happier for it. This game is far from perfect, but for fans of tactical RPGs it is a truly a diamond in the rough. Battles are varied and interesting and party composition and tactical choices really make a difference. The combat system is deeper than it first appears and that hidden depth is one of the games finer qualities. It is also it's biggest drawback. The game is closely based on a pen and paper RPG and unfortunately in many ways just as indecipherable to the beginner. The character progression system is almost arcane in its complexity, to the point that it is almost certain that you will make mistakes in the way you build up your party. These mistakes will be deadly on even normal difficulty. It's reliance on a pen and paper system mean that unless you have a copy of the rulebook and many hours to ponder it and try out permutations, your characters will be woefully shy of optimal. This may lead to you having to restart the game several times as you begin to unravel its mysteries. That being said , the game is sufficiently fun, interesting and challenging that you won't mind having to restart. I didn't.
